title: The Binomial Distribution and Hypothesis Testing
seo_title: Year 12 A Level Maths: Binomial Distribution Worksheets
standard_text: Understand and use the binomial distribution as a model; calculate probabilities using the binomial distribution; understand and apply the language of statistical hypothesis testing (null and alternative hypotheses, significance level, critical region, p-value) for a binomial proportion.
meta_desc: Free Year 12 A level maths worksheets on the binomial distribution and hypothesis testing: P(X = r), P(X ≤ r), the mean np, null and alternative hypotheses and one-tailed tests. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: X ~ B(n, p): P(X = r) = ⁿCᵣ pʳ (1 − p)ⁿ⁻ʳ.
key_sub: Reject H₀ when the p-value is less than the significance level.
body_html:
How it works

X ~ B(n, p) when there are n independent trials, each with the same probability p of success. E(X) = np.

A hypothesis test: H0: p = p0; H1: p > p0 or p < p0. Find the probability of a result at least as extreme as the one observed; if it is below the significance level, reject H0.

Example

X ~ B(5, 0.5). P(X = 2)?

⁵C₂ × 0.5² × 0.5³ = 10 ÷ 32

Answer: 0.3125

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting the ⁿCᵣ factor.
  • Using P(X = r) instead of P(X ≥ r) in a test.
  • Saying H₁ is 'proved'.

faq.q: When can you use a binomial model?
faq.a: When there is a fixed number of independent trials, each with two outcomes and the same probability of success.
The result would be unlikely if H₀ were true, so there is evidence for H₁. It does not prove H₁.
